new_statements.rule_in_words: Per the author of the Sawila grammar, word stress in Sawila is lexicalized (phonemic, not predictable by a single positional rule); vowel length is also phonemic. The open first-hand source gives no positional detail. Schapper 2020 (second-hand survey, HAL ms p.18) characterizes Sawila as one of the AP languages with a low-functional-load phonemic stress system in which stress regularly falls on heavy syllables, while in disyllables consisting of two light syllables stress is lexical and may be on either the first or second syllable of the root.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in either accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: None in the first-hand remark. Schapper 2020's survey formulation implies weight-driven placement (heavy syllables attract stress) with lexical placement only in all-light disyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: One-sentence typological remark about the word-level prosodic system; no discussion of phrase level or citation forms. The full treatment is in Kratochvíl 2014 'Sawila' sketch grammar (De Gruyter), not accessible from our machine.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted first-hand statement (Kratochvíl 2014, APL 012) is about Sawila as a whole (sawi1256), made jointly with Abui. Caution on Donohue 1996 'Inverse in Tanglapui' (LLM 27), which Glottolog attaches to sawi1256 by computerized assignment: its data are from the Lantoka dialect of Tanglapui, and Schapper 2020:4 identifies Tanglapui (Stokhof 1975, Donohue 1996) as a Kula-speaking clan, so its footnote 'Stress is non-contrastive, and initial' (p.101 fn.1) describes Kula (kula1280), not Sawila; it is saved in the sawi1256 folder with this caveat recorded in and could serve a kula1280 entry instead.

sources.note: p.124 sec.1.1 (typological profile): Abui and Sawila have 'phonemic vowel length and lexicalized stress found in both languages, and marginal tone found in Abui'. No positional rule; first-hand remark by the author of the Sawila sketch grammar.

sources.citation: Schapper, Antoinette. 2020. Introduction to The Papuan languages of Timor, Alor and Pantar, Volume III. In A. Schapper (ed.), The Papuan languages of Timor, Alor and Pantar: Sketch grammars, vol. 3, 1-52. De Gruyter Mouton. HAL author version halshs-02930405.
sources.note: ms p.18 (PDF p.19), sec.5.1: Sawila listed with Nedebang, Teiwa, Kamang among AP languages with 'phonemic stress systems bearing low functional loads'; common pattern: stress regularly falls on heavy syllables, but in disyllables of two light syllables stress is lexicalized and may fall on the first or second syllable of the root. Second-hand survey statement (primary = Kratochvíl 2014 sketch). Also p.4: 'Tanglapui' (Stokhof 1975, Donohue 1996) is the name of one of four Kula-speaking clans.
